You'd never expect a face on Mars.
But in 1976, NASA's Viking 1 photographed one, 1.5 kilometers wide. What was it, actually?
That's the first of six strange things found in our solar system.
For each one, we'll look at what spacecraft and telescopes actually found, and give an honest verdict: solved, best guess, or still unknown.
Number one: the face on Mars.
In July 1976, NASA's Viking 1 orbiter was taking pictures of Mars, looking for a safe place to land its twin, Viking 2.
In a region called Cydonia, one picture showed something odd. A huge rock formation that looked like a human head, with eyes, a nose, and a mouth.
NASA's own caption at the time already explained it: the face was formed by shadows, giving the illusion of eyes, nose, and mouth.
The sun was low, at about 20 degrees. And the photo was full of tiny errors, which made it look even more like a face.
But the picture took on a life of its own. Books, magazines, and later websites claimed it was a monument built by an ancient Martian civilization.
More than twenty years later, new spacecraft went back with much sharper cameras.
In 2001, NASA's Mars Global Surveyor photographed the same spot. And in 2007, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter took an even closer look.
The face was gone. In its place was an ordinary eroded hill, a mesa, like many others in the same region.
NASA's conclusion: a natural looking Martian hill whose illusory face-like appearance depends on the viewing angle and the angle of the light.
Our brains are built to find faces everywhere. Scientists call it pareidolia. It's the same reason you sometimes see a face in a cloud or on the front of a car.
Verdict: solved. It's a hill, and a trick of the light.
Number two: the moon with two faces.
Saturn has a moon called Iapetus. And it looks like it was painted by two different artists.
One side is as dark as coal. The other side is bright white, like fresh snow.
Astronomers noticed this more than 300 years ago. Giovanni Cassini, who discovered Iapetus in 1671, could only see it on one side of Saturn.
When the moon was on the other side of its orbit, it seemed to disappear. Its dark half was facing us.
In 2007, NASA's Cassini spacecraft, named after him, flew close to Iapetus. And it found a strange runaway process.
It starts with dust. Dark material spirals in from moons farther out from Saturn, and Iapetus runs into it head-on, like a car driving into rain. That darkens the side that faces forward.
Then the Sun takes over. A dark surface absorbs more sunlight and warms up. On the warm side, ice slowly turns into vapor.
That vapor drifts away and freezes again on colder, brighter areas. So the bright parts get brighter, and the dark parts lose their ice and get darker.
A Cassini scientist called Iapetus the victim of a runaway feedback loop, operating on a global scale.
Iapetus has one more oddity: a giant ridge running along its equator, like the seam on a walnut. That one is still being debated. But the two colors have a clear explanation.
Verdict: solved. Dust from outside, and a runaway game of ice and sunlight.
Number three: the hexagon on Saturn.
At Saturn's north pole, the clouds form a giant six-sided shape. A hexagon.
It was first seen when the Voyager spacecraft flew past Saturn in 1980 and 1981.
When Cassini arrived in 2004, the north pole was in its long winter darkness. Saturn's year lasts about 29 Earth years, so each season lasts more than seven.
Cassini first saw the hexagon using infrared, which picks up heat from Saturn's warm interior. Later, when spring came, it finally saw it in sunlight.
The hexagon is about 30,000 kilometers across. That's more than twice as wide as Earth. And winds inside it race at about 500 kilometers an hour.
In the middle sits a giant storm, with an eye about fifty times larger than a typical hurricane on Earth.
So what is the hexagon? It's a jet stream. A river of fast-moving air, bent into six sides.
Scientists even made a hexagon in a lab, using a spinning tank of water. They also got squares, octagons, and other shapes, depending on the speed and the fluid.
But two questions remain. Why does Saturn have a hexagon only in the north, and not in the south? And why does it last so long?
A Cassini scientist pointed out that weather features like this are notoriously turbulent and unstable. Yet the hexagon has held its shape for decades.
Verdict: best guess. It's a jet stream, but nobody knows why it's so stable.
Number four: the visitor from another star.
On the nineteenth of October 2017, a telescope in Hawaii spotted a small object racing away from the Sun.
It was moving too fast to be from our solar system. It was the first object ever confirmed to come from interstellar space.
It was named ʻOumuamua, a Hawaiian word for scout.
It was small, somewhere between about 100 and 1,000 meters long, and probably very elongated. And it was already leaving.
Then astronomers noticed something strange. As it moved away from the Sun, it sped up slightly, more than gravity alone could explain.
Comets do this. When the Sun warms them, they release gas, and the gas pushes them like a little rocket. But comets also grow a fuzzy glowing cloud and a tail.
ʻOumuamua showed neither.
That gap left room for wild ideas. One Harvard astronomer even explored the idea that it was artificial, a thin solar sail.
In 2023, two scientists offered a simpler answer in the journal Nature.
They suggested ʻOumuamua began as a lump of ice. During millions of years in interstellar space, cosmic rays turned some of that water ice into trapped hydrogen gas.
When it came close to the Sun and warmed up, that hydrogen escaped. Too little to see, but enough to give a small object a gentle push.
Lab experiments show this kind of hydrogen does form when ice is hit by radiation. But we can't go back and check. ʻOumuamua is long gone.
Verdict: best guess. Probably an icy object releasing hydrogen. It's the best explanation so far, but it hasn't been confirmed.
Number five: the methane on Mars.
On Earth, a lot of methane is made by living things, like microbes. So when NASA's Curiosity rover detected methane on Mars, people got excited.
It could mean microbes. Or it could come from rocks, water, and heat deep underground.
Curiosity measures tiny amounts in Gale Crater, less than half a part per billion on average. NASA compared it to a pinch of salt in an Olympic swimming pool.
But sometimes, the methane suddenly jumps, up to about 20 parts per billion.
Then the European Trace Gas Orbiter arrived. It was built to be the gold standard for measuring gases on Mars. And it saw no methane at all.
The scientist leading Curiosity's methane instrument said: I was definitely shocked.
So who was right? Maybe both.
Curiosity's instrument needs a lot of power, so it mostly works at night. At night, the Martian air is calm, so methane seeping from the ground can build up near the surface.
During the day, the Sun stirs the air, and the methane gets mixed so thin that the orbiter can't see it.
That explains part of the puzzle. It doesn't explain where the methane comes from, or why it spikes, or why it doesn't seem to build up over time.
Verdict: still unknown. The timing makes sense, but the source is a mystery.
Number six: a gas in the clouds of Venus.
Venus is a brutal place. The surface is hot enough to melt lead.
But high up in its clouds, the temperature and pressure are closer to Earth's. Some scientists have wondered if microbes could survive there.
In September 2020, a team announced they had detected phosphine in Venus's clouds, using the ALMA and JCMT radio telescopes.
On Earth, phosphine is linked to life. And no known non-living process on a rocky planet makes it in large amounts.
The news went around the world.

Then other teams checked the data. They found calibration problems. When ALMA released corrected data, the phosphine signal became much weaker, around one part per billion instead of the twenty first reported.
Some researchers argued the signal could be sulfur dioxide instead.
The original team still says no other molecule fits as well. Others have proposed volcanoes as a source.
So, is there phosphine on Venus or not? Scientists are still arguing.
Verdict: still unknown. The detection is disputed, and future missions will have to check.
So, let's check the scoreboard.
The face on Mars: solved. A hill and a trick of the light.
Iapetus's two faces: solved. Dust and a runaway loop of ice and sunlight.
Saturn's hexagon: best guess. A jet stream, but strangely stable.
ʻOumuamua: best guess. Probably an icy body releasing hydrogen.
Methane on Mars: still unknown.
Phosphine on Venus: still unknown.
Two solved, two best guesses, and two we still can't explain. Our own solar system still has plenty of secrets.
